title: The system: warehouse inventory and shipping that reserves and ships exactly once
caption: Every call that changes stock or buys a label carries a key the server remembers; every event carries an id the consumer remembers. Retries and redeliveries then cost nothing.

steps.text: A shopper checks out. The order service creates one Idempotency-Key per reservation (derived from the order and line, not from the HTTP attempt) and sends it with the reserve call.
The Inventory API claims the key, decrements available stock, and saves the reply and an outbox row, all in one transaction in the inventory DB.
The call times out on the order service's side, so it retries with the same key. The API finds the finished key and returns the stored reply: one reservation, however many attempts.
Once the parcel is packed, fulfilment buys a shipping label from the carrier, passing the shipment id as the carrier's reference, and records the label plus an outbox row.
The relay reads both outboxes and publishes stock-reserved and label-created, each with a stable event id. It may publish an event twice; consumers expect that and skip ids they have already handled.
Every night the reconciler matches the carrier's invoice lines to label rows by reference. A label we were billed for but never recorded, or one billed twice, becomes a ticket to void it.

scenarios.name: Flash sale
scenarios.summary: A limited drop slows the inventory DB, timeouts multiply and so do retries. Keys turn every retry into a lookup, so no unit is reserved twice and the stock count stays honest.

steps.text: A sneaker drop opens and reserve calls jump twentyfold. Row locks on the hot SKU push latency past the order service's timeout.
Each timed-out call is retried with its original key, with backoff and jitter so the retries don't arrive as one wave.
A retry that arrives while the first attempt still holds the lease gets 409 with Retry-After; it never queues on the hot row.
A retry after the commit gets the stored reply. Stock left equals units sold, and the picking app sees each reservation once.

scenarios.name: Inventory DB failover
scenarios.summary: The primary dies and an async replica takes over, losing its last commits. Because key, reservation and outbox row were one transaction, they disappear together and the retry simply redoes the work.

steps.text: The inventory primary crashes; the promoted replica is missing the last second of commits.
One lost commit held a reservation, its finished key and its stock-reserved outbox row. All three are gone, never half of them.
The order service never got a reply, so it retries with the same key. The new primary has no record of it, so it is claimed fresh and stock is reserved exactly once.
Had the key lived in a separate store, it could survive while the reservation vanished, and the retry would replay a reply for stock nobody holds.

scenarios.name: Key made per attempt
scenarios.summary: A refactor moves key creation inside the retry loop. Every retry now looks new; a unique constraint on the reservation is what stops double holds while the deploy is rolled back.

steps.text: A cleanup of the HTTP client generates a fresh key on each attempt instead of once per reservation. Tests pass: they never time out.
In production the first timeout sends a second key for the same order line. To the Inventory API it is a brand-new request.
The second insert hits UNIQUE(order_id, line) on reservations and is refused, so no extra stock is held. The backstop does the key's job.
A spike in unique-constraint errors pages the team, and the deploy is rolled back. Add a test that retries with a timeout.
